data.text/markdown:
Geodetic coordinates: WGS84, ECEF, ENU and UTM

This notebook uses the MRPT Python wheel (pip install mrpt3) to convert GNSS positions between the coordinate systems used in outdoor robotics, with the mrpt.topography module:
  • TGeodeticCoords, TCoords: latitude, longitude and height on the WGS84 ellipsoid.
  • geodeticToGeocentric_WGS84(), geocentricToGeodetic(): Earth-Centered, Earth-Fixed (ECEF) coordinates.
  • geodeticToENU_WGS84(), ENUToGeodetic_WGS84(), ENU_axes_from_WGS84(): local East-North-Up (ENU) frames.
  • geodeticToUTM(), UTMToGeodetic(): the UTM map projection.
Pick a place and a survey loop size: everything below is recomputed. Try Greenwich or the equator to see UTM break, and large loops to see the Earth curvature in ENU.

data.text/html: Parameters

data.text/markdown:
1. One point, four coordinate systems

  • Geodetic (WGS84): latitude, longitude and height above the WGS84 ellipsoid, as given by any GNSS receiver. Angles are not metric: a degree of longitude shrinks with the latitude.
  • ECEF: Cartesian (x, y, z) in meters, with the origin at the Earth center, z toward the North pole and x toward longitude 0°. Global and metric, but its axes have nothing to do with the local horizontal.
  • ENU: Cartesian frame tangent to the ellipsoid at a reference point: x East, y North, z Up. It is just ECEF rotated and translated (ENU_axes_from_WGS84() gives that rigid transform).
  • UTM: a map projection. The Earth is split into 60 zones of 6° of longitude, each one projected onto a plane (easting, northing). The letter is the latitude band (C to X, from South to North), not the hemisphere: bands N and above are in the northern one.

data.text/markdown:
2. A GNSS survey loop

Now we simulate a surveyor (or a robot) driving a closed loop around the reference point, logging 360 GNSS fixes (latitude, longitude, and the same ellipsoidal height as the reference). Each fix is converted to ENU, ECEF and UTM with MRPT, and then back to geodetic to check the round trips.

data.text/html:
Loop length computed in Length (m) Difference (m)
ECEF (true 3D distances) 71,336.925
ENU (x, y, z) 71,336.925 -0.000
UTM (easting, northing) 71,310.223 -26.703
ENU keeps distances exactly, because it is a rigid transformation of ECEF: transforming the ECEF points with the pose from ENU_axes_from_WGS84() gives the same ENU coordinates (max. difference 1.6e-06 mm). UTM does not: its scale factor goes from 0.9996 at the zone central meridian to about 1.001 at the zone edges, and it measures on the ellipsoid surface, not at the actual height. Its grid North also differs from true North by -0.322° here (meridian convergence). Worst round-trip errors back to geodetic: ENU 2.8e-06 mm, ECEF 2.8e-06 mm, UTM 1.5e-06 mm.

data.text/markdown:
Why robots use local ENU frames

Robot navigation, SLAM and sensor fusion need a metric, Cartesian frame where x and y are horizontal and z is vertical: ENU is exactly that around its origin, with no projection distortion and no zone boundaries. Geodetic angles are not metric, ECEF has no notion of "up", and UTM distorts distances and breaks at zone and hemisphere boundaries. ENU is a plane tangent to a curved Earth, though: points at a constant height drop below it as ||(d^2 / (2 R)||), about 8 cm at 1 km and 8 m at 10 km (right plot). So ENU frames are kept local: a few kilometers around a reference point, typically the first GNSS fix of the mission. Larger areas are split into several local frames.

Run it on your computer (Linux, Python 3.11 to 3.14): 
uvx marimo edit --sandbox https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MRPT/mrpt-notebooks/main/notebooks/geodetic_coordinates.py
More MRPT Python examples: mrpt_examples_py.
